plain_english_title: PTSD Stressor Rules, Military Sexual Trauma (MST) Markers & Non-PTSD Mental Health Claims
what_this_means: Under 38 C.F.R. § 3.304(f), how VA verifies an in-service traumatic event ('stressor') for Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) depends on which of five pathways applies: (1) PTSD diagnosed during active service, (2) combat service, (3) fear of hostile military or terrorist activity, (4) Former Prisoner of War captivity, or (5) in-service personal assault or Military Sexual Trauma (MST). Because assaults are rarely reported in official military channels, § 3.304(f)(5) and federal court rulings (AZ v. Shinseki; Menegassi v. Shinseki) forbid VA from treating the absence of an official report as evidence the assault did not happen, and allow corroboration through 'markers'—subtle changes in behavior, work performance, health visits, or statements to friends and family. Equally important, non-PTSD mental health diagnoses such as Major Depressive Disorder or Generalized Anxiety Disorder are governed by direct service connection (38 C.F.R. § 3.303(a)) rather than § 3.304(f)'s PTSD stressor corroboration rules.
record_clues: A VA denial discounting a Veteran's account of Military Sexual Trauma or personal assault because no contemporary military police or medical report appeared in Service Treatment Records.

A PTSD denial for 'uncorroborated stressor' when VA or private records simultaneously diagnosed Major Depressive Disorder (Diagnostic Code 9434), Generalized Anxiety Disorder (Diagnostic Code 9400), or Panic Disorder (Diagnostic Code 9412) linked to service.

Personnel or medical file clues ('markers') such as a sudden drop in performance evaluations, uncharacteristic disciplinary actions (Article 15 / non-judicial punishment), requests to transfer units or duty stations, emergency clinic or screening visits, significant weight changes, or an early 'personality disorder' discharge.

Service on or near a base, convoy route, ship, or airspace exposed to mortar, rocket, IED, or sniper threats where PTSD was denied before July 13, 2010, or denied later without an exam by a VA or VA-contracted psychiatrist or psychologist (§ 3.304(f)(3)).
important_cautions: Key effective date for 'fear of hostile activity': VA's liberalizing rule in 38 C.F.R. § 3.304(f)(3) took effect July 13, 2010 (published at 75 FR 39843 and formally corrected from July 12 to July 13, 2010 at 75 FR 41092). Because it is a prospective liberalizing rule, it cannot be used to prove Clear and Unmistakable Error (CUE) in final decisions issued before July 13, 2010, and it specifically requires confirmation by a VA or VA-contracted psychiatrist or psychologist (upheld in NOVA v. Secretary of Veterans Affairs).

Newly obtained official military unit histories, deck logs, morning reports, or military investigative files (CID/NCIS/AFOSI) that corroborate a previously denied PTSD or MST stressor can unlock retroactive reconsideration back to the original claim date under 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(c).

VA's February 15, 2022 mental health rating proposal (RIN 2900-AQ82, 87 FR 8498) remains an unfinalized proposed rule and is NOT enacted law; existing DSM-5 criteria under 38 C.F.R. § 4.130 remain in force.

Under George v. McDonough and 38 C.F.R. §§ 20.1403(d)–(e) and 20.1409(c), disputes over how an adjudicator weighed marker evidence cannot establish CUE, and only one final merits CUE decision is allowed per prior Board decision issue.
questions_for_representative: If my PTSD claim was denied for lack of stressor corroboration, did the examiner also diagnose depression, anxiety, or another DSM-5 mental disorder that should have been evaluated under 38 C.F.R. § 3.303(a) (Clemons v. Shinseki / Patton v. West)?

Have we requested my complete Official Military Personnel File (OMPF)—including performance marks, transfer requests, and disciplinary records—to identify behavioral markers under 38 C.F.R. § 3.304(f)(5)?
Could official unit logs, deck logs, or archival stressor records trigger retroactive reconsideration of an earlier denial under 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(c)?

If my stressor involved fear of hostile military or terrorist activity, did a VA or VA-contracted psychiatrist or psychologist evaluate whether the event is consistent with the places, types, and circumstances of my service under § 3.304(f)(3)?
